learn.hook: A cotton boll fresh from a Gujarat field is worth a few rupees. Spun, woven and stitched into a shirt, it's worth hundreds. That jump is value addition.
points: Secondary activities add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products.

Example: cotton in the boll has limited use; turned into yarn and then fabric, it becomes more valuable. Iron ore cannot be used directly from the mine; converted into steel, it gains value and can make machines and tools.
Secondary activities include manufacturing, processing and construction (infrastructure) industries.
They connect primary activities (which supply raw materials) to tertiary activities (which distribute and service the products).

example.q: Trace how value is added when sugarcane becomes packaged sugar.
steps: Sugarcane is grown (primary activity).
A sugar mill crushes cane and crystallises sugar (secondary — processing/manufacturing).
The sugar is worth more than the raw cane — value has been added.
example.answer: Crushing and refining in a mill add value to sugarcane

learn.hook: From a Moradabad brass lamp to an ISRO rocket — both are 'manufactured'. What do they have in common?
points: Manufacturing involves a full array of production — from handicrafts to moulding iron and steel, stamping out plastic toys, and assembling delicate computer components or space vehicles.
Manufacturing literally means 'to make by hand'; today it also includes goods 'made by machines'.
Common characteristics of modern manufacturing: application of power, mass production of identical products, and specialised labour in factory settings producing standardised commodities.
Industry is a broader term than manufacturing — we speak of the tourism industry or entertainment industry, which do not manufacture goods. Manufacturing is one part of industry.
Factory production workers are commonly called blue-collar workers.

steps: Manufacturing = making goods from raw materials.

But 'industry' is broader (tourism/hospitality industry) → yes, part of industry.
example.answer: Not manufacturing, but part of the (tourism) industry

learn.hook: In a modern car plant, a robot welds, a computer checks quality and one worker tightens the same bolt all day. Why organise work like this?
points: Specialisation of skills/methods: the craft method makes only a few made-to-order pieces at high cost; mass production makes large quantities of standardised parts, with each worker doing only one task repeatedly.

Mechanisation: using gadgets to do tasks. Automation — without the aid of human thinking during manufacturing — is the advanced stage; automatic factories have feedback and closed-loop computer control systems where machines 'think'.
Technological innovation through research and development (R&D) for quality control, eliminating waste and inefficiency, and combating pollution.
Organisational structure and stratification: complex machine technology, extreme specialisation and division of labour, vast capital, large organisations and an executive bureaucracy.
Uneven geographic distribution: major concentrations cover less than 10 per cent of the world's land area; these nations have become centres of economic and political power.

topics.title: Location of industries: market, raw material, labour and energy

learn.hook: Why are India's sugar mills in cane fields, but its aluminium smelters near power plants? Every industry has its own magnet.
points: Industries maximise profits by cutting costs, so they locate where production costs are lowest.

Access to market: the existence of a market is the most important factor. Developed regions (Europe, North America, Japan, Australia) have large purchasing power; densely populated developing regions are also large markets. Some industries such as aircraft and arms have global markets.

Access to raw material: raw materials should be cheap and easy to transport. Industries using cheap, bulky, weight-losing materials (ores) locate near the source — steel, sugar and cement; perishables (agro-processing, dairy) are processed close to the source.
Access to labour: mechanisation, automation and flexible processes have reduced dependence on labour, but some industries still need skilled labour.
Access to energy: industries that use a lot of power locate near energy sources — e.g. the aluminium industry; coal was the main source earlier, now hydroelectricity and petroleum are also important.

example.q: Why are sugar mills in India located in sugarcane-growing areas?
steps: Sugarcane is bulky and loses weight on processing (weight-losing).
It also dries and loses sucrose quickly after cutting (perishable).
Locating mills near fields cuts transport cost and loss.
example.answer: Sugarcane is weight-losing and perishable, so mills are near the fields

topics.title: Location of industries: transport, government policy and agglomeration

learn.hook: Why do auto-part makers crowd around Maruti's plant in Gurugram–Manesar? Being close to the leader pays off.
points: Access to transportation and communication: speedy and efficient transport carries raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets; transport costs play a big role. Western Europe and eastern North America have highly developed transport systems, which has always encouraged concentration of industries there.
Communication is also needed to exchange and manage information.
Government policy: governments adopt 'regional policies' to promote 'balanced' economic development and set up industries in particular (often backward) areas, offering incentives.

Access to agglomeration economies: many industries benefit from nearness to a leader industry and other industries; these benefits are called agglomeration economies. Savings arise from links between industries.

example.q: Explain why many small component makers cluster around a big car plant.
steps: The car plant (leader industry) buys their components.
Being near cuts transport time and cost.
Shared roads, power and skilled labour reduce costs for all — agglomeration economies.
example.answer: They gain agglomeration economies from nearness to the leader industry

learn.hook: A diamond-polishing unit can work in Surat, a chip-design lab in Bengaluru, and both could just as well be elsewhere. Their 'feet' are loose!
points: Footloose industries can be located in a wide variety of places; they are not dependent on any specific raw material, weight-losing or otherwise.
They largely depend on component parts that can be obtained anywhere.
They produce in small quantities, employ a small labour force and are generally non-polluting.

learn.hook: A potter's wheel in a Khurja courtyard, a power loom shed in Bhiwandi and the giant Tata Steel works — three scales of manufacturing.
points: Manufacturing industries are classified on the basis of size, inputs/raw materials, output/products and ownership.

Household or cottage manufacturing: the smallest unit; artisans use local raw materials and simple tools at home with family members or part-time labour; products for home use, local (village) markets or barter; capital and transport matter little. Examples: pottery, basket weaving, handicrafts.

Small-scale manufacturing: in a workshop outside the home; local raw materials, simple power-driven machines and semi-skilled labour; provides employment and raises local purchasing power. India, China, Indonesia and Brazil developed labour-intensive small-scale manufacturing.
Large-scale manufacturing: large market, various raw materials, enormous energy, specialised workers, advanced technology, assembly-line mass production and large capital.
Major large-scale manufacturing regions: Great Lakes region of the USA, Western Europe, Eastern Europe and Japan; newer centres include Brazil, China, India and South Korea.

example.q: Classify: (a) a family making bamboo baskets at home for the village haat; (b) a workshop with 15 workers and electric looms; (c) an automobile plant with assembly lines.
steps: (a) Home, family labour, local market → household/cottage.
(b) Workshop outside home, simple power machines → small scale.
(c) Assembly line, huge capital → large scale.

topics.title: Classification by inputs: agro, mineral, chemical, forest and animal based

learn.hook: Your morning tea, your notebook, your shoes and your cement house all come from different kinds of industries — sorted by what they're made from.
points: Agro-based industries process raw materials from fields and farms: food processing, sugar, pickles, fruit juices, beverages (tea, coffee, cocoa), spices, oils and fats, textiles (cotton, jute, silk) and rubber.

Food processing includes canning, producing cream, fruit processing and confectionery. Agri-business is commercial farming on an industrial scale, often financed by businesses whose main interests lie outside agriculture.
Mineral-based industries: ferrous metallic minerals (iron and steel), non-ferrous metals (aluminium, copper, jewellery) and non-metallic minerals (cement, pottery).
Chemical-based industries use naturally occurring chemical minerals — mineral oil (petroleum) for petrochemicals; salts, sulphur and potash; also synthetic fibres and plastics.
Forest-based industries use timber for furniture, wood, bamboo and grass for paper, and lac; animal-based industries use hides and skins for leather, wool for woollens, and ivory from elephant tusks.

example.q: Classify: jute bags, aluminium foil, plastic buckets, paper, woollen shawls.
steps: Jute bags → agro-based (textile).
Aluminium foil → mineral-based (non-ferrous).
Plastic buckets → chemical-based.
Paper → forest-based.
Woollen shawls → animal-based.
example.answer: Agro, mineral, chemical, forest, animal based respectively

topics.title: Classification by output and by ownership

learn.hook: Steel from SAIL ends up inside your fridge; the fridge itself is a consumer good. Who owns each factory? That's another way to classify.
points: Basic industries: their products are used to make other goods; e.g. iron and steel used to make machinery, which in turn makes other goods.
Consumer goods industries: produce goods consumed directly — bread and biscuits, tea, soaps and toiletries, paper for writing, televisions, etc.

Public sector industries: owned and managed by governments; India has many Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs); socialist countries have many state-owned industries; mixed economies have both public and private sector enterprises.
Private sector industries: owned by individual investors or private organisations; capitalist countries have mostly private enterprises.
Joint sector industries: managed by joint stock companies, or by the private and public sectors together.

example.q: Classify: (a) SAIL's Bhilai Steel Plant; (b) a biscuit factory owned by a private company; (c) Maruti Udyog when it was set up by the government with Suzuki.
steps: (a) Government-owned; makes steel used in other industries → public sector, basic industry.
(b) Private owners; goods eaten directly → private sector, consumer goods.
(c) Government + private partner → joint sector.
example.answer: (a) public & basic, (b) private & consumer, (c) joint sector

learn.hook: Silicon Valley near San Francisco began in orchards; today its low glass buildings design the chips inside billions of phones.
points: High-technology (high-tech) industry is the latest generation of manufacturing: it applies intensive research and development (R&D) to make products of an advanced scientific and engineering character.
Professional (white-collar) workers make up a large share of the workforce and greatly outnumber production (blue-collar) workers.

Examples: robotics on assembly lines, computer-aided design (CAD) and manufacturing, electronic controls of smelting and refining, and constant development of new chemical and pharmaceutical products.

The high-tech landscape has neatly spaced, low, modern, dispersed office-plant-lab buildings rather than massive assembly structures; planned business parks for start-ups are part of development schemes.

Regionally concentrated, self-sustained, highly specialised high-tech clusters are called technopolis — e.g. Silicon Valley near San Francisco and Silicon Forest near Seattle. Manufacturing overall (iron and steel, textiles, automobiles, petrochemicals, electronics) contributes significantly to the world economy.
